VIA E-TARIFF

Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, NE
Washington, DC 20426

          Re:     The Connecticut Light and Power Company, Docket No. ER27-_______

                  Respectfully Requesting an Order on or before January 10, 2027

Dear Secretary Reese:

         Pursuant to sections 219 and 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”),1 Part 35 of the
regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”),2 and
Order No. 679,3 The Connecticut Light and Power Company (“CL&P”) requests authorization to
recover 100% of the prudently incurred costs associated with CL&P’s investment in a transmission
project at the Huntsbrook Junction in eastern Connecticut (“Huntsbrook Project” or “the Project”)
if the Project is abandoned or canceled, in whole or in part, for reasons beyond the control of CL&P
(“Abandoned Plant Incentive”).

I.        INTRODUCTION

         The Huntsbrook Project is a forward-looking transmission investment designed to expand
the hosting capacity of the New England transmission system and enable the interconnection of up
to 2,400 MW of new generation resources, which also increases transfer capability on critical
transmission interfaces in the state and region. By proactively addressing anticipated transmission
constraints, the Huntsbrook Project will enhance the reliability and resilience of the New England
electric system, reduce congestion, facilitate the efficient integration and delivery of new energy
resources, and support regional resource adequacy objectives. The Abandoned Plant Incentive
requested herein is a necessary component of advancing the Huntsbrook Project and realizing these
reliability, economic, and resource adequacy benefits for consumers and developers throughout
New England. Given the substantial development risks associated with a large-scale, forward-
looking transmission investment of this nature, the Huntsbrook Project is unlikely to proceed
absent Commission approval of the requested Abandoned Plant Incentive.

       The Huntsbrook Project was developed through a collaborative, anticipatory planning
process involving ISO New England Inc. (“ISO-NE”) and the New England states to address the
region’s evolving resource adequacy, reliability, and energy needs. Consistent with federal and
regional policy objectives supporting proactive transmission development, the U.S. Department of
Energy (“DOE”) selected the Huntsbrook Project as a key component of the Power Up New
England portfolio for a federal funding award now totaling approximately $371 million. The New
England states and project participants are currently finalizing the award with DOE. In addition,
CL&P is authorized to state that the New England States Committee on Electricity (“NESCOE”)
and the Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources (“MA DOER”), which is acting as the
lead DOE grant applicant and prime recipient for the Power Up award on behalf of the participating
New England states, support CL&P’s request for the Abandoned Plant Incentive as an important
mechanism for reducing the risks associated with development of the Huntsbrook Project.

        Against this backdrop, CL&P requests approval of the Abandoned Plant Incentive for the
Huntsbrook Project pursuant to section 219 of the FPA, as implemented by the Commission in
Order No. 679, and, in the alternative, pursuant to section 205 of the FPA. Approval of the
requested incentive is warranted because the Huntsbrook Project is a forward-looking transmission
investment that will improve the reliability of the New England transmission system, reduce the
cost of delivered power to consumers by reducing transmission congestion, and facilitate the
efficient integration of new generation and storage resources needed to meet the region’s growing
electricity needs. As demonstrated in the testimony of Jacob Lucas, Vice President of
Transmission System Planning at Eversource Energy Service Company, submitted as
Attachment A with this filing (“Lucas Testimony”), the Project will increase the transfer capability
of two critical Connecticut transmission interfaces that deliver power to the densely populated
southwestern Connecticut load pocket and that contain facilities essential to the reliable operation
of the bulk electric system. In addition, as demonstrated in the testimony of Benjamin D’Antonio,
Director of Economic Analysis and Transmission Strategy at Eversource Energy Service
Company, submitted as Attachment B with this filing (“D’Antonio Testimony”), and the
supporting economic analysis, the Project will provide substantial congestion relief, reliability,
and resource enablement benefits to New England consumers.

        This filing also addresses the concerns identified by the Commission in its order denying
without prejudice CL&P’s prior request for the Abandoned Plant Incentive for the Huntsbrook
Project.4 In that order, the Commission found that CL&P had not yet provided a sufficient
evidentiary record demonstrating that the Huntsbrook Project would ensure reliability or lower the
cost of delivered power through congestion reduction. This filing remedies those deficiencies and
presents a comprehensive factual record demonstrating that the Project satisfies the standards
established by section 219 and Order No. 679. In particular, this filing includes new evidence
regarding the Project’s reliability benefits, a detailed congestion analysis quantifying reductions
in wholesale energy costs, and additional information concerning the Project’s development risks
and its role in facilitating future resource development in New England.

       The requested incentive is justified on multiple independent grounds.

         First, the Huntsbrook Project qualifies for the rebuttable presumption established in Order
No. 679 because it was selected through a fair, open, and transparent planning process involving
both a competitive solicitation conducted by the New England states and an independent
evaluation by DOE. As discussed in Section III.A.1, that process evaluated the Project’s
reliability, economic, and transmission benefits and shares the fundamental characteristics of
planning processes that the Commission previously has found sufficient to support the rebuttable
presumption.

         Second, even apart from the rebuttable presumption, the record independently
demonstrates that the Huntsbrook Project satisfies section 219’s statutory requirements. As
discussed in Sections III.A.2 and III.A.3, the Project will increase transfer capability into
Connecticut and the southwestern Connecticut load pocket, improve transmission system
performance and operational flexibility, reduce fault exposure affecting critical generation
facilities, reduce transmission congestion, lower locational marginal prices, and reduce wholesale
energy costs paid by New England consumers. The Commission has repeatedly found similar
reliability and congestion reduction showings sufficient to support incentive treatment under
section 219.

        Third, as discussed in Sections III.B.1 through III.B.3, the requested incentive
independently advances important Commission policy objectives that justify incentive approval
under section 205. The Huntsbrook Project will create a resource-neutral 345 kV interconnection
hub capable of accommodating up to 2,400 MW of new generation and storage resources, thereby
helping address growing resource adequacy challenges identified by ISO-NE, the North American
Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”), DOE, and the Commission itself. The Project also
reflects the type of forward-looking and anticipatory transmission planning encouraged by Order
Nos. 1920 and 2023, the Trump Administration’s Speed to Power initiative, and recent
Commission efforts to address accelerating load growth and interconnection challenges.

        Fourth, as discussed in Section III.B.4, the Huntsbrook Project has received extraordinary
support from both the New England states and DOE. The Project was selected for inclusion in the
Power Up New England portfolio, which is supported by up to $371 million in DOE funding. The
New England states, acting through NESCOE and MA DOER, have continued to support
implementation of the Project and have expressly endorsed CL&P’s request for the Abandoned
Plant Incentive as an appropriate mechanism to reduce development risk and facilitate timely
project advancement.

        Finally, as discussed in Section III.C, the requested incentive is appropriately tailored to
the specific risks and challenges associated with developing the Huntsbrook Project. Those risks
include uncertainties associated with DOE funding implementation, the New England states’
termination rights, future ISO-NE study outcomes, permitting and siting requirements, supply
chain and construction constraints, and the substantial upfront investments required long before
the Project begins providing service. The requested incentive is narrowly targeted to mitigate
those risks and is therefore consistent with the nexus requirement established in Order No. 679
and the Commission’s Incentives Policy Statement.
 Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
November 10, 2026

        Accordingly, the Commission should grant the requested Abandoned Plant Incentive
because the Huntsbrook Project satisfies the requirements of section 219 and Order No. 679 and,
independently, promotes important Commission policies under section 205 by encouraging
development of a strategically significant transmission project that will improve reliability, reduce
consumer costs, facilitate future resource development, and support the long-term needs of the
New England electric system. CL&P requests that the Commission approve the requested
Abandoned Plant Incentive effective January 10, 2027, that being 61 days after the date of this
filing. Commission action by that date is critical to the Huntsbrook Project because the Project is
currently participating in the ISO-NE Cluster Study process, and January 19, 2027, is the deadline
to withdraw from that cluster. That deadline provides CL&P with a finite opportunity after
Commission action on this filing to evaluate the Project’s viability and determine whether to
continue participation before incurring additional costs and financial exposure.

II.       BACKGROUND

          A.     CL&P

         CL&P, a subsidiary of Eversource Energy (“Eversource”),5 is a public utility that owns and
operates transmission and distribution facilities in the state of Connecticut. CL&P’s transmission
facilities are subject to the operating control of ISO-NE pursuant to the Transmission Operating
Agreement (“TOA”) by and among ISO-NE and the New England Participating Transmission
Owners, including CL&P, and CL&P provides transmission service pursuant to the terms of
Section II of the ISO-NE Transmission, Markets and Services Tariff (“ISO-NE OATT”).6
Eversource Energy Service Company, a service company subsidiary of Eversource, provides
various corporate services to Eversource’s subsidiaries, including CL&P.

          B.     The Huntsbrook Project

         The Huntsbrook Project is a new 345 kV switching station
at the Huntsbrook Junction in eastern Connecticut (shown right).
The Project will enable the interconnection of up to 2,400 MW of
new generation resources to the New England transmission system
without necessitating significant additional upgrades of the existing
transmission system. By increasing the transmission grid’s hosting
capacity for new generation and relieving congestion at a strategic
location on the 345 kV network, the Huntsbrook Project will
facilitate critical additions to New England’s energy supply needed
to meet growing demand, support resource adequacy, enhance

supply diversity, and improve reliability by reducing electric system reliability risks, particularly

        The Huntsbrook Project is strategically located within an existing transmission right of way
at the intersection of multiple transmission corridors. The Project will utilize 345 kV, 3000A,
63 kA equipment in a breaker-and-a-half configuration consisting of two adjacent three-bay yards
and will bisect five existing and overlapping 345 kV transmission lines originating from the
Millstone Nuclear Power Station (“Millstone”) and Montville Generating Station (“Montville”),
resources that are critical to maintaining regional reliability during peak demand and extreme
winter conditions. The location therefore provides reliability benefits that accrue to customers
throughout New England by improving planners’ and operators’ ability to manage risks associated
with faults on several long and overlapping transmission lines. In addition, by reconfiguring the
348 and 364 lines, which form part of the Western Connecticut Import Interface, the Project will
increase transfer capability by approximately 181 MW across the Connecticut Import Interface
and approximately 144 MW across the Western Connecticut Import Interface, strengthening the
transmission paths that deliver power to the densely populated southwestern Connecticut load
pocket.7

        The Huntsbrook Project is one component of a broader regional initiative known as Power
Up New England (“Power Up”), an integrated portfolio of projects developed through a
collaboration among project developers, including Eversource, ISO-NE, and the six New England
states to address the region’s evolving reliability and resource adequacy needs. Power Up’s
transmission investments include the Huntsbrook Project and the Brayton Point Project in
Massachusetts, which is being developed by National Grid. These projects are designed to
strategically prepare the transmission system for future generation development by creating points
of interconnection in advance of project-specific needs, thereby accelerating the integration of new
resources onto the grid. Together, the Huntsbrook Project and the Brayton Point Project will ready
the New England transmission system for the interconnection of up to 4,800 MW of new
generation capacity.

        Power Up also includes Form Energy’s Multi-Day Iron-Air Battery project, an 85
MW/8,500 MWh advanced multi-day storage facility to be constructed in Maine. The facility will
be capable of continuously dispatching electricity for 100 hours, providing up to four days of
backup power to the region during periods of prolonged cold weather and other system events. As
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright recognized during his recent visit to Form Energy’s project
site in Maine, “[i]t’s energy storage that’s matched with the problem.”8 In addition to enhancing
system reliability, the battery project will reduce curtailment in a transmission-constrained area
and represents the redevelopment of a former paper mill brownfield site using domestically
manufactured technology. DOE has identified the battery component as a particularly significant
element of the Power Up portfolio because it demonstrates a replicable, innovative approach to

       Collectively, the Power Up portfolio is expected to relieve congestion at strategic locations
on the regional transmission system, facilitate the timely interconnection of new generation
resources, improve system reliability, strengthen resource adequacy, and reduce wholesale energy
supply costs for New England customers by about $1.55 billion.

        Power Up is supported through DOE’s Grid Innovation Program (“GIP”), which is
administered under the Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships (“GRIP”) Program established
pursuant to Section 40103(b) of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (“IIJA”).
Congress established Section 40103(b) specifically to support projects that enhance electric system
resilience and reliability through strategic investments in transmission, storage, and other grid
infrastructure.9

        In response to a September 2023 solicitation from the New England states for projects
eligible for GIP funding, Eversource submitted the Huntsbrook Project for consideration.
Following a competitive evaluation process, the New England states selected the Project for
inclusion in the Power Up proposal submitted to DOE. After DOE encouraged the proposal to
proceed to the full application stage, the New England states, Eversource, National Grid, Form
Energy, and ISO-NE submitted a full Power Up application in April 2024. On August 6, 2024,
DOE announced its selection of the Power Up proposal for federal funding. Since that time, the
New England states and project partners, including Eversource, have worked closely with DOE to
finalize the funding award. As part of those collaborative efforts, and in response to evolving
market conditions and policy priorities, Eversource revised the scope of the Huntsbrook Project to
function as a resource-neutral point of interconnection rather than a point of interconnection
dedicated to a single resource. On August 18, 2026, MA DOER reached agreement with DOE on
the terms and conditions of the $371 million funding agreement and is now working to finalize
that agreement, as well as subrecipient agreements with Eversource and the other project partners.

        The Huntsbrook Project is estimated to cost approximately $237 million. Through the
Power Up award, CL&P expects to receive approximately $69 million of DOE grant funding to
offset project costs.10 Funds received from DOE will be used as credits to reduce CL&P’s
investment in the Project, thereby lowering the costs included in rate base and reducing the annual
transmission revenue requirement paid by customers. CL&P will seek recovery of the remaining
Project costs through separate Commission filings establishing a cost recovery mechanism under

        The Huntsbrook Project currently has a projected in-service date of August 2034.
Achieving that schedule is critical to maintaining compliance with Power Up funding milestones
and preserving eligibility for DOE funding. Accordingly, Eversource must proceed expeditiously
with Project development activities. Timely approval of the Project will support Eversource’s

Cluster Study processes, and help avoid delays that could jeopardize Project milestones, funding
objectives, and the anticipated reliability and generation integration benefits of the Huntsbrook
Project.

III.       REQUEST FOR ABANDONED PLANT INCENTIVE

         CL&P respectfully requests that the Commission approve the Abandoned Plant Incentive
for the Huntsbrook Project pursuant to section 219 of the FPA and Order No. 679. The Huntsbrook
Project is a forward-looking transmission investment that will improve transmission system
reliability, reduce the cost of delivered power by alleviating transmission congestion, and facilitate
the integration of new generation and storage resources needed to meet New England’s evolving
electricity needs. As discussed below, the requested incentive is warranted because the
Huntsbrook Project qualifies for Order No. 679’s rebuttable presumption, independently satisfies
the statutory requirements of section 219 through its reliability and congestion-reduction benefits,
advances important Commission policies supporting anticipatory transmission development and
resource adequacy, has received significant support from both the New England states and DOE,
and presents development risks for which the requested Abandoned Plant Incentive is
appropriately tailored under the Commission’s nexus standard.

           A.       The Abandoned Plant Incentive Is Consistent with Section 219 and Order
                    No. 679.

        Pursuant to Order No. 679, an applicant may seek to obtain incentive rate treatment for a
transmission infrastructure investment that satisfies the requirements of section 219, i.e., the
applicant must show that “the facilities for which it seeks incentives either ensure reliability or
reduce the cost of delivered power by reducing transmission congestion.”12 Order No. 679
established the process for an applicant to demonstrate that it meets this standard, including a
rebuttable presumption that the standard is met if: (1) the transmission project results from “a fair
and open regional planning process that considers and evaluates [the] project[] for reliability and/or
congestion and is found to be acceptable to the Commission;” or (2) “a project has received
construction approval from an appropriate state commission or state siting authority.”13 The

        The Abandoned Plant Incentive requested for the Huntsbrook Project is consistent with the
requirements of FPA section 219 and Order No. 679. As demonstrated below, the Project satisfies
the statutory standard through multiple independent avenues.

         First, the Huntsbrook Project qualifies for Order No. 679’s rebuttable presumption because
it was selected through a fair, open, and transparent planning process that evaluated the Project’s
reliability and economic benefits. Specifically, the Huntsbrook Project was chosen through a two-
stage review process consisting of a competitive solicitation conducted by the participating New
England states and an independent evaluation by DOE, a process that bears the same essential
characteristics as the alternative planning frameworks the Commission has previously held qualify
for the rebuttable presumption.

        Second, even apart from the rebuttable presumption, the record demonstrates that the
Huntsbrook Project independently satisfies section 219’s reliability requirement. As demonstrated
in the Lucas Testimony, the Project will increase the transfer capability of the Connecticut Import
Interface and the Western Connecticut Import Interface—both of which contain facilities
associated with established Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits (“IROLs”)—by
approximately 181 MW and 144 MW, respectively, enhancing the ability to deliver power into
southwestern Connecticut, an area ISO-NE has identified as a key area of concern for load-serving
capability. In addition, by inserting a new 345 kV switching station at Huntsbrook Junction, the
Project will reduce transmission-system fault exposure on critical transmission facilities serving
eastern Connecticut, significantly decrease the circuit-mile risk associated with faults affecting
major generating resources, and provide system operators with enhanced operational flexibility for
maintenance, restoration, and outage management. These benefits constitute direct and
measurable improvements to transmission-system reliability.

         Third, the Huntsbrook Project independently satisfies section 219’s congestion-reduction
requirement. As demonstrated by the economic analysis presented in the D’Antonio Testimony,
the Huntsbrook Project will increase hosting capacity at a strategic location on the 345 kV system,
facilitate the interconnection and delivery of substantial quantities of new generating resources,
reduce transmission congestion, lower locational marginal prices across New England, and reduce
wholesale energy costs paid by consumers. The analysis further demonstrates that these
congestion reduction benefits are consistent with, and supported by, Commission precedent
granting incentive treatment for transmission projects designed to accommodate future generation
development and reduce the cost of delivered power.

       Accordingly, whether viewed through the rebuttable presumption established in Order No.
679 or on the basis of the Project’s independently demonstrated reliability and congestion relief

                  1.      The Huntsbrook Project Resulted from a Fair and Open Regional
                          Planning Process.

         Order No. 679 established a rebuttable presumption that a transmission project satisfies the
statutory requirement of ensuring reliability and/or reducing congestion if the project “result[s]
from a fair and open regional planning process that considers and evaluates [the] project[] for
reliability and/or congestion and is found to be acceptable to the Commission.”15 In applying this
standard, the Commission has focused on two fundamental considerations: (1) whether the
planning process evaluates projects for reliability and/or congestion benefits, and (2) whether the
process is fair and open, meaning that it is transparent and provides meaningful opportunities for
stakeholder participation.16

        The Commission has made clear that the rebuttable presumption is not limited to projects
selected through a traditional RTO reliability planning process. Rather, the Commission has
extended the presumption to alternative transmission planning frameworks where those same core
characteristics are present.

       For example, in Mid-Atlantic Offshore Development, LLC and similar PJM orders, the
Commission found that PJM’s State Agreement Approach (“SAA”) qualified for the rebuttable
presumption even though it operated outside PJM’s traditional Regional Transmission Expansion
Planning (“RTEP”) process and was designed primarily to address state public-policy objectives.17
The Commission explained that the relevant inquiry was not whether the process mirrored the
RTEP, but whether it evaluated transmission projects for reliability and congestion benefits
through a fair and transparent process.18 The Commission concluded that the SAA satisfied that
standard because it evaluated whether the proposed projects would ensure reliability and/or reduce
congestion and because PJM employed an open and transparent solicitation.19

         Likewise, in ITC Midwest LLC and similar MISO/SPP orders, the Commission held that
the Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue (“JTIQ”) Study conducted by MISO and SPP qualified
for the rebuttable presumption.20 Although the JTIQ Study was not part of either RTO’s traditional

solutions for reliability and congestion benefits and incorporated extensive stakeholder
engagement, including multiple opportunities for stakeholder review and input.21

        These decisions establish an important principle: the rebuttable presumption turns on the
substance of the planning process, not the label attached to it. Where a planning process evaluates
transmission projects for reliability or congestion benefits through procedures that are fair, open,
and transparent, the Commission has found the requirements of Order No. 679 satisfied regardless
of whether the process is a traditional RTO planning process.

        The Huntsbrook Project was selected through such a rigorous review process that included
both state-led screening and DOE’s independent competitive evaluation under the GIP. Although
this process differs from a traditional RTO reliability planning proceeding, it incorporates many
of the same features the Commission has found relevant under Order No. 679, including
independent review, competition among alternative proposals, and an express focus on reliability
and resilience benefits. Indeed, the development of the Huntsbrook Project is an example of an
anticipatory planning and development approach similar to the longer-term transmission planning
process for the New England states that was accepted by the Commission after the states submitted
their grant application to DOE.22

an invitational call seeking project concepts for potential inclusion in a regional application for

evaluated competing proposals and scored them according to criteria designed to identify projects
most likely to satisfy DOE’s funding requirements while advancing regional policy objectives.24

        That emphasis on reliability was not incidental. Congress established the GIP to support
projects that enhance grid reliability and resilience through innovative transmission, storage, and

applications that would “improve grid reliability and resilience on the local, regional, and
interregional scales” and identified as a priority projects that “improve the reliability and resilience

        Following the initial state review based on DOE’s FOA criteria, the New England states
selected the Huntsbrook Project for inclusion in the Power Up New England portfolio submitted
to DOE in December 2023.29 The Project then underwent a second, independent evaluation
conducted by DOE pursuant to Section 40103(b) of the IIJA.

        DOE’s review process was both competitive and merit-based. The FOA established a two-
phase evaluation process in which DOE first conducted an “independent assessment” of submitted
concept papers and encouraged only a subset of applicants to advance to the full application

locations that they know will require significant network upgrades to enable interconnection.

        Prior to the reforms required by Order No. 2023, interconnection customers could enter the
queue with minimal financial commitment and limited demonstration of project viability, leading
to severe backlogs—by the end of 2022, there were over 10,000 active interconnection requests

remain in the queue. The rule significantly increased financial readiness requirements and
imposed withdrawal penalties on customers whose exit from the queue materially impacts other

withdrawing party rather than other queue participants.93

Attachment A
Testimony of Jacob Lucas
                         UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                               BEFORE THE
                 FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION




The Connecticut Light and Power Company   )   Docket No. ER27-_______




                     TESTIMONY OF JACOB LUCAS
      ON BEHALF OF THE CONNECTICUT LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
                                                                                         Page 1 of 14



 1   I.   INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.   Please state your name and business address.

 3   A.   Jacob Lucas, 56 Prospect Street, Hartford, CT 06103.


 4   Q.   By whom are you employed and in what capacity?

 5   A.   I am the Vice President of Transmission System Planning at Eversource Energy Service

 6        Company (“Eversource”). In this role, I oversee the planning and development of the

 7        three-state transmission system owned and operated by Eversource’s public utility

 8        affiliates, including the studies used to assess system performance and the reliability

 9        impacts of proposed transmission projects. I direct the reliability analyses that determine

10        the need for and scope of transmission investments across Eversource’s transmission

11        system and coordinate the development of both near-term and long-term plans to address

12        Eversource and regional bulk power system needs.


13   Q.   Does your role include the evaluation of transmission projects that will be owned and

14        operated by The Connecticut Light and Power Company?

15   A.   Yes.   Eversource’s transmission assets are owned and operated by its public utility

16        affiliates, including The Connecticut Light and Power Company (“CL&P”). In my

17        testimony, I will generally refer to Eversource and intend that to include CL&P.


18   Q.   Please describe your professional and educational background.

19   A.   Prior to my current role, I was the Director of Transmission System Planning at Eversource,

20        where my responsibilities included directing reliability studies that established the need

21        and scope for transmission projects across the three-state Eversource transmission system
                                                                                          Page 2 of 14


 1        and coordinating the development of short-term and long-term plans to address the region’s

 2        bulk power system needs. Prior to that I was the Manager of Transmission Interconnections

 3        where my responsibilities included managing interconnection service requests across the

 4        three-state Eversource system to ensure reliability of service.       Prior to working at

 5        Eversource I worked at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or

 6        “Commission”), where I managed the Engineering and Planning West Group within the

 7        Division of Engineering , Planning, and Operations in the Office of Electric Reliability.

 8        My responsibilities at the Commission included directing and performing technical and

 9        policy analyses, including load flow, stability, and production cost modeling for

10        Commission orders to support bulk power system reliability. Prior to that I was an

11        electrical engineer with the Commission and a Senior Transmission Line Engineer with

12        NSTAR Electric & Gas.

13   A.   I have an electrical engineering degree from the University of North Carolina and a Master

14        of Science, Power Systems Management from Worcester Polytechnic Institute.


15   Q.   Have you previously provided testimony to FERC?

16   A.   No.


17   Q.   Please explain the purpose of your testimony.

18   A.   I am submitting this Testimony in support of CL&P’s request for authorization from FERC

19        to recover 100% of the prudently incurred costs associated with CL&P’s investment in a

20        transmission project at the Huntsbrook Junction in eastern Connecticut (“Huntsbrook

21        Project” or “the Project”) if the Project is abandoned or canceled, in whole or in part, for

22        reasons beyond the control of CL&P (“Abandoned Plant Incentive”). Specifically, my
                                                                                          Page 3 of 14


 1         testimony explains how the Huntsbrook Project will provide reliability benefits to

 2         Connecticut and the broader New England electric grid by increasing the transfer capability

 3         of two critical Connecticut transmission interfaces.


 4   Q.    How is your testimony organized?

 5   A.    I first provide an overview of the Huntsbrook Project and the system goals that informed

 6         its development. I then describe the Transfer Limit Analysis (“TLA”) that Eversource

 7         performed to evaluate the Project, including the study methodology, planning case, and

 8         assumptions used. Next, I present the results of the TLA. Finally, I explain why the

 9         increased transfer capability provided by the Project improves the reliability of the bulk

10         electric system serving Connecticut and New England.


11   II.   OVERVIEW OF THE HUNTSBROOK PROJECT

12   Q.    Please describe the Huntsbrook Project.

13   A.    The Huntsbrook Project is a new 345 kV switching station at the Huntsbrook Junction in

14         eastern Connecticut. The Project is strategically located within an existing transmission

15         right-of-way at the intersection of two large transmission rights-of-way containing five

16         separate 345 kV transmission lines that originate from the Millstone Nuclear Power Station

17         (“Millstone”) and the Montville Generating Station (“Montville”).

18                The Project consists of the addition of sixteen 345 kV circuit breakers and the

19         construction of two independent 345 kV switchyards at the Huntsbrook Junction location,

20         utilizing 345 kV, 3000A, 63 kA equipment in a breaker-and-a-half configuration consisting

21         of two adjacent three-bay yards. The existing 310, 348, 364, 371, and 383 lines will be

22         bifurcated and looped into the new switchyards, creating new two-terminal lines between
                                                                                     Page 4 of 14


 1   the Huntsbrook Junction and the Manchester, Millstone, Haddam, Haddam Neck,

 2   Montville, and Card substations. The new two-terminal 345 kV lines that will result from

 3   the Project are identified in Table 1 below.

 4   Table 1: New Two-Terminal 345 kV Lines Created by the Huntsbrook Project

                      Existing Line             New Two-Terminal Line
                          310               Manchester to Huntsbrook Junction
                          310                Millstone to Huntsbrook Junction
                          348                Haddam to Huntsbrook Junction
                          348                Millstone to Huntsbrook Junction
                          364              Haddam Neck to Huntsbrook Junction
                          364               Montville to Huntsbrook Junction
                          371               Montville to Huntsbrook Junction
                          371                Millstone to Huntsbrook Junction
                          383                  Card to Huntsbrook Junction
                          383                Millstone to Huntsbrook Junction


 5          Rather than operating as long, uninterrupted circuits between their existing

 6   terminals, each of these lines will terminate at the new Huntsbrook Junction switchyards,

 7   providing new switching and fault clearing capability at this critical location on the 345 kV

 8   network.

 9          The Huntsbrook Project will also enable the interconnection of up to 2,400 MW of

10   new generation resources to the New England transmission system. The economic,

11   congestion relief, and resource adequacy benefits of the Project are addressed in the

12   testimony of Benjamin D’Antonio, which is submitted as Attachment B to CL&P’s filing.

13   My testimony focuses on the reliability benefits associated with the Project’s effect on the

14   transfer capability of the Connecticut transmission system.
                                                                                            Page 5 of 14


 1   Q.     What system goals were considered when developing the Huntsbrook Project

 2          concept?

 3   A.     The Huntsbrook Project is intended to add new transmission switching and fault clearing

 4          functionality at a critical intersection of two large transmission rights-of-way containing

 5          five separate 345 kV lines. This new functionality will allow the integration of new future

 6          generation and will also provide reliability benefits to the transmission system.        In

 7          particular, by reconfiguring the 348 and 364 lines, which form part of the Western

 8          Connecticut Import Interface, the Project modifies the configuration of that interface in a

 9          manner that increases the transfer capability of both the Western Connecticut Import

10          Interface and the Connecticut Import Interface.


11   III.   THE TRANSFER LIMIT ANALYSIS

12   Q.     What is a Transfer Limit Analysis?

13   A.     A TLA is a transmission planning study used to determine the maximum amount of electric

14          power that can be reliably transferred from one area of the bulk electric system to another

15          while maintaining compliance with applicable reliability criteria under both normal and

16          contingency conditions. This maximum amount of reliable transfer is referred to as the

17          transfer limit.

18                  In transmission system planning, electric power does not flow along a single path

19          between a source and a load. Rather, power flows according to the electrical characteristics

20          of the interconnected network and distributes itself across many transmission facilities

21          simultaneously. As a result, increasing transfers between areas may increase loading on

22          transmission facilities and may negatively affect system reliability. The objective of a TLA

23          is to identify the transfer capability of the transmission system and to determine which
                                                                                           Page 6 of 14


 1        transmission facilities and reliability criteria limit additional transfers. The analysis

 2        evaluates the performance of the transmission system as power transfers are incrementally

 3        increased between a defined source area and a defined sink area.


 4   Q.   Why is a Transfer Limit Analysis important from a transmission planning

 5        perspective?

 6   A.   A TLA serves several important purposes.          It helps planners identify transmission

 7        constraints, evaluate the impact of generation additions or retirements, assess interregional

 8        transfer capability, support transmission needs assessments, and evaluate the benefits of

 9        proposed transmission projects. By identifying the facilities that constrain power transfers,

10        the analysis provides insight into where transmission reinforcements may increase system

11        capability and improve overall system flexibility and reliability.


12   Q.   Did Eversource perform a Transfer Limit Analysis to evaluate the Huntsbrook

13        Project?

14   A.   Yes. Eversource’s Transmission System Planning group, which I oversee, completed a

15        TLA to evaluate the impact of the Huntsbrook Project on the transfer capability of the

16        Connecticut transmission system. My testimony describes the methodology, assumptions,

17        and results of that analysis.


18   Q.   Which transmission interfaces did the Transfer Limit Analysis evaluate?

19   A.   The TLA evaluated two major interfaces in Connecticut: the Connecticut Import Interface

20        and the Western Connecticut Import Interface. Because the 348 and 364 lines are part of

21        the Western Connecticut Import Interface and will be modified by the Project to create two-

22        terminal lines terminating at the Huntsbrook Junction switchyards, the TLA evaluated both
                                                                                           Page 7 of 14


 1        the pre-Project and post-Project configurations of the Western Connecticut Import

 2        Interface. The post-Project configuration of the interface includes the portion of the 348

 3        line between Haddam and the Huntsbrook Junction and the portion of the 364 line between

 4        Haddam Neck and the Huntsbrook Junction. The Connecticut Import Interface definition

 5        is the same before and after the Project.


 6   Q.   What software did Eversource use to perform the analysis, and why?

 7   A.   Eversource used PowerGEM’s Transmission Adequacy and Reliability Assessment

 8        (TARA) planning software to perform the transfer analysis. Inherent in this software is the

 9        ability to create incremental increases in transfers across defined interfaces in the network

10        model and to identify the transfer values at which transmission elements become

11        overloaded. A proportional transfer analysis was performed to determine the Project’s

12        maximum incremental transfer capability.

13               The TARA software performs a DC transfer analysis to establish incremental

14        transfer limit values. However, a DC transfer analysis does not take into account the

15        reactive component of the power flow. For this reason, the TARA software includes an

16        inherent AC verification, which Eversource used to obtain accurate and final incremental

17        transfer values.


18   Q.   What system planning case was used in the analysis, and why?

19   A.   The analysis was based on ISO New England Inc.’s (“ISO-NE”) 2034 Summer Evening

20        Peak load case. This case was selected because it was specifically developed to support

21        area review assessments in Connecticut, including the region affected by the Huntsbrook

22        Project.
                                                                                             Page 8 of 14


 1   Q.   How was the planning case set up for the analysis?

 2   A.   To assess the transfer capability of the affected interfaces under stressed import conditions,

 3        the generation dispatch in the case was modified to create an east-to-west power flow bias

 4        in the New England transmission system. This dispatch pattern increased imports into

 5        Connecticut and enabled evaluation of the maximum import capability of both the Western

 6        Connecticut Import Interface and the Connecticut Import Interface. In addition, relevant

 7        generating units in Western Massachusetts were turned on to stress the system from

 8        Western Massachusetts into Connecticut.

 9               Transfers were established with the source located east of the Western Connecticut

10        Import Interface and the sink located mostly within the bounds of the Southwest

11        Connecticut electrical subarea. To increase transfer levels in the case, a set of generators

12        in the source area was ramped up while, at the same time, a set of generators in the sink

13        area was ramped down, in each case in the ratio of their maximum outputs. Two initial

14        dispatches were developed, one with the Millstone generating units in service and one with

15        the Millstone units out of service, and the Millstone units were excluded from the sink.


16   Q.   Which generating units were included in the source and sink subsystems?

17   A.   Three subsystems were created for the N-1 and N-1-1 testing: a sink subsystem for the

18        Millstone-in-service dispatch, a sink subsystem for the Millstone-out-of-service dispatch,

19        and a source subsystem. The sink units, which were on in the initial base case, were

20        incrementally turned down as transfers increased, and the source units, which were off in

21        the initial base case, were ramped up as transfers increased, in each case in the ratio of their

22        maximum outputs.
                                                                                           Page 9 of 14


 1   Q.    What contingency conditions were evaluated?

 2   A.    The TLA determined both the N-1 and N-1-1 transfer limits for the post-Project system.

 3         The N-1 transfer analysis was performed using contingencies deemed impactful to the

 4         Connecticut Import and Western Connecticut Import interfaces, and transmission elements

 5         in these areas were monitored as part of the transfer analysis. For the N-1-1 analysis, each

 6         of the 345 kV lines in Connecticut was assumed to be out of service as the first element

 7         out.   The transfer limit was identified as the transfer level at which a monitored

 8         transmission element reached 100% of its Long-Term Emergency rating.


 9   IV.   RESULTS OF THE TRANSFER LIMIT ANALYSIS

10   Q.    What were the results of the Transfer Limit Analysis?

11   A.    The TLA demonstrates that the Huntsbrook Project will increase transfer capability by

12         approximately 181 MW (an approximately 8% increase) across the Connecticut Import

13         Interface and by approximately 144 MW (an approximately 3% increase) across the

14         Western Connecticut Import Interface, without overloading any relevant transmission

15         element above 100% of its Long-Term Emergency rating.

16                More specifically, before reaching the thermal limit of the first limiting element,

17         the Connecticut Import Interface transfer limit increases from 2,154.4 MW without the

18         Project to 2,335.2 MW with the Project, an increase of 180.8 MW (8.3%). The Western

19         Connecticut Import Interface transfer limit increases from 4,288.3 MW without the Project

 4   V.      RELIABILITY BENEFITS OF THE HUNTSBROOK PROJECT

 5   Q.      Why are the Connecticut Import and Western Connecticut Import interfaces

 6           important to Connecticut and New England from a reliability perspective?

 7   A.      The Connecticut Import Interface and the Western Connecticut Import Interface are critical

 8           to the reliable operation of Connecticut’s transmission system and the New England bulk

 9           electric system. The Connecticut Import Interface facilitates both imports needed to serve

10           Connecticut load and exports that support load elsewhere in New England and the broader

11           Northeast, including transfers to and from New York. The Western Connecticut Import

12           Interface is also a key operational constraint that is actively monitored in real time to ensure

13           system reliability.
                                                                                       Page 11 of 14




 1

 2               Both interfaces include facilities associated with established Interconnection

 3        Reliability Operating Limits (“IROLs”), underscoring their importance to maintaining

 4        reliable bulk power system operations. They are particularly critical because the majority

 5        of power serving southwestern Connecticut must flow across these interfaces. As a result,

 6        they provide essential transmission pathways for delivering generation located elsewhere

 7        in Connecticut and New England to the heavily concentrated load pocket in southwestern

 8        Connecticut, which sits at the end of the New England transmission system near the New

 9        York border.


10   Q.   How does the additional transfer capability provided by the Huntsbrook Project

11        improve reliability?

12   A.   The Huntsbrook Project improves reliability by increasing transfer capability across the

13        Connecticut Import Interface and the Western Connecticut Import Interface, two

14        transmission pathways that are critical to serving load in southwestern Connecticut. As

15        discussed earlier, southwestern Connecticut is heavily dependent on power delivered over
                                                                                        Page 12 of 14


 1   the transmission system from generation resources located elsewhere in Connecticut and

 2   New England.

 3            The importance of these interfaces is expected to grow over time. In its 2050

 4   Transmission Study Report, ISO-NE identified load-serving capability in southwestern

 5   Connecticut as a key area of concern.1 That challenge is expected to become more

 6   significant as fossil-fueled generation retires and electric demand increases due to

 7   economic development, transportation electrification, and the widespread adoption of heat

 8   pumps.

 9            By increasing transfer capability across both interfaces, the Huntsbrook Project will

10   enhance the ability to serve future load growth while maintaining reliable system

11   operations and compliance with applicable reliability criteria. These improvements are

12   particularly important in southwestern Connecticut, where demand growth is expected to

13   be greatest and where opportunities to develop new local generation are limited. The

14   additional transfer capability will allow more power to be delivered into this load pocket,

15   improving reliability, strengthening operational flexibility, and helping ensure that future

16   electricity needs can be met efficiently and reliably. In addition, because both interfaces

17   contain facilities associated with established IROLs, the Project’s ability to increase

18   transfer capability across these interfaces while maintaining acceptable loading on IROL-

19   related facilities represents a significant reliability benefit of the Project.

 2        from the increased transfer limits?

 3   A.   Yes. ISO-NE has identified a need for increased transfer capability into southwestern

 4        Connecticut. In its 2050 Transmission Study, ISO-NE evaluated the future transmission

 5        system using criteria established by the North American Electric Reliability Corporation

 6        (“NERC”), including Reliability Standard TPL-001, ISO-NE Planning Procedure No. 3,

 7        and Northeast Power Coordinating Council, Inc. (“NPCC”) Directory #1. Based on that

 8        analysis, ISO-NE identified load-serving capability in southwestern Connecticut as a key

 9        area of concern.

10               The Connecticut Import Interface and the Western Connecticut Import Interface are

11        critical transmission pathways for delivering power into southwestern Connecticut. By

12        increasing transfer capability across both interfaces, the Huntsbrook Project will increase

13        the amount of power that can be delivered into that load pocket while maintaining reliable

14        system operations. As a result, the Project will help address the need identified by ISO-

15        NE and improve the transmission system’s ability to serve future load growth in

16        southwestern Connecticut.


17   Q.   Please summarize the reliability benefits of the Huntsbrook Project discussed in your

18        testimony.

19   A.   The Huntsbrook Project will increase the transfer capability of the Connecticut Import

20        Interface by approximately 181 MW and of the Western Connecticut Import Interface by

21        approximately 144 MW, without overloading any relevant transmission element above

22        100% of its Long-Term Emergency rating. These interfaces contain IROL-related facilities

23        that are essential to the reliable operation of the bulk electric system and serve as critical
                                                                                       Page 14 of 14


1        pathways for delivering power to the southwestern Connecticut load pocket, an area that

2        ISO-NE has identified as a key area of concern for load-serving capability.             By

3        strengthening these transmission paths, the Project will enhance the ability of the

4        transmission system to reliably serve future load growth in Connecticut and will improve

5        the reliability and operational flexibility of the bulk electric system serving Connecticut

6        and New England.


7   Q.   Does this conclude your Testimony?

8   A.   Yes, it does.

 1   I.   INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.   Please state your name and business address.

 3   A.   Benjamin D’Antonio, 780 North Commercial Street, Energy Park, Manchester, NH 03101.


 4   Q.   By whom are you employed and in what capacity?

 5   A.   I am the Director of Economic Analysis and Strategy at Eversource Energy Service

 6        Company (“Eversource”). I lead an internal economic analysis group focused on power

 7        sector modeling that examines power sector impacts associated with transmission

 8        development and resource adequacy. In this capacity, I advance the concept development

 9        of early-stage strategic transmission projects with an emphasis on establishing the business

10        case and commercialization strategy for the projects and identifying potential regulatory

11        and legal issues. I also advise and represent Eversource on wholesale market participation

12        strategies in the New England Power Pool and provide subject matter expertise related to

13        interconnection, transmission, and power sector trends.


14   Q.   Does your role include development of transmission projects that will be owned and

15        operated by The Connecticut Light and Power Company?

16   A.   Yes.   Eversource’s transmission assets are owned and operated by its public utility

17        affiliates, including The Connecticut Light and Power Company (“CL&P”). In my

18        testimony, I will generally refer to Eversource and intend that to include CL&P.


19   Q.   Please describe your professional and educational background.

20   A.   Prior to becoming the Manager and then Director of Economic Analysis and Strategy at

21        Eversource, I was Senior Counsel and Analyst at the New England States Committee on
                                                                                          Page 2 of 31



 1        Electricity (“NESCOE”), where I advised and represented state policymakers and

 2        regulators on federal energy issues through a diverse range of analytical, legal, and

 4        England states, the development of a multi-faceted resource and infrastructure planning

 5        study that analyzed the future state of the regional power system with a focus on resource

 8        Division at the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities and an Energy and

 9        Environment Fellow at the Regulatory Assistance Project. I have degrees in economics,

10        law, and environmental policy.


11   Q.   Have you previously provided testimony to the Federal Energy Regulatory

12        Commission (“FERC”)?

13   A.   Yes, I provided testimony on behalf of CL&P in Docket No. ER25-747.


14   Q.   Please explain the purpose of your testimony.

15   A.   I am submitting this testimony in support of CL&P’s request for authorization from FERC

16        to recover 100% of the prudently incurred costs associated with CL&P’s investment in a

17        transmission project at the Huntsbrook Junction in eastern Connecticut (“Huntsbrook

18        Project” or “the Project”) if the Project is abandoned or canceled, in whole or in part, for

19        reasons beyond the control of CL&P (“Abandoned Plant Incentive”).
                                                                                          Page 3 of 31



 1   Q.    Have you been involved in the development of the Huntsbrook Project?

 2   A.    Yes. My colleagues and I have been leading the development of the Huntsbrook Project

 3         for Eversource. As part of that effort, I have led Eversource’s engagement with the New

 4         England states, both directly and through NESCOE, to advance the Huntsbrook Project.


 5   Q.    How is your testimony organized?

 6   A.    I first provide a brief overview of the New England region’s changing energy needs, federal

 7         funding opportunities for innovative transmission projects, and the Huntsbrook Project. I

 8         then describe Eversource’s process for identifying the Huntsbrook Project and work with

 9         the New England states to secure federal funding. I then discuss the benefits of the

10         Huntsbrook Project, which include reduced transmission congestion, lower cost of

11         delivered power for New England consumers, and enhanced reliability and resilience of

12         the regional electric grid. Next, I discuss two risks faced by the Huntsbrook Project—

13         permitting and siting risks and supply chain risks. Finally, I address the use of advanced

14         technologies.



15   II.   BACKGROUND

16   Q.    Please briefly describe the New England region’s changing energy needs.

17   A.    The New England region faces significant challenges that are driving a need for additional

18         generation interconnection capacity. In the coming decade, the ISO New England Inc.

19         (“ISO-NE”) region is expected to experience significant demand growth as the system peak

20         shifts from summer to winter due to increased building and transportation electrification.
                                                                                     Page 4 of 31



 1              In its 2026 Regional Electricity Outlook, ISO-NE identifies energy adequacy and

 2   robust transmission as foundational requirements for maintaining reliability as

 3   transportation electrification, building electrification, economic growth, and other factors

 4   increase regional electricity demand.1 ISO-NE further explains that New England must

 5   prepare for significant load growth while simultaneously integrating new resources capable

 6   of meeting reliability requirements.

 7              NERC’s most recent Long-Term Reliability Assessment likewise identifies

 8   growing risks associated with ensuring that sufficient resources and supporting

 9   infrastructure are available to serve future demand reliably, particularly during periods of

10   system stress.2 For New England specifically, NERC identified an elevated risk level for

11   2029 onward because “[s]trong demand growth and persistent winter natural gas

12   infrastructure limitations pose risks of energy shortfalls in extreme winter conditions.”3

13              These reliability concerns have recently been demonstrated in actual system

14   operations.      During a prolonged period of extreme cold between January 23 and

15   February 10, 2026, ISO-NE reported that temperatures averaged approximately 11.3°F

16   below normal throughout the nineteen-day event, resulting in elevated demand, record

 1                  Taken together, these trends demonstrate that New England’s electricity system is

 5        infrastructure necessary to efficiently and reliably connect those resources to the regional

 6        grid.      Expanding generation interconnection capability is therefore an important

 7        component of ensuring that New England can maintain reliability while supporting the

 8        region’s long-term energy needs.


 9   Q.   Please briefly describe the federal funding opportunities available for innovative

10        transmission projects designed to advance grid resilience and reliability.

11   A.   Funded through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (“IIJA”) and administered by

12        the U.S. Department of Energy’s (“DOE”) Grid Deployment Office, the Grid Innovation

13        Program (“GIP”) supports projects that use innovative approaches to transmission, storage,

14        and distribution infrastructure to enhance grid resilience and reliability.8 Consistent with

15        the program’s statutory purpose, the GIP is designed to coordinate and collaborate with

16        electric sector owners and operators to demonstrate innovative transmission, storage, and

17        distribution infrastructure that hardens and enhances grid resilience and reliability, as well

18        as new approaches to improving regional grid resilience through cost-shared projects

                                                                                                 Page 7 of 31



 1        implemented by states, public entities, and rural electric cooperatives.9 The GIP will invest

 2        up to $5 billion, and projects are subject to a 50% cost share requirement. The first funding

 3        cycle of the GIP concluded on October 18, 2023. The second funding cycle concluded on

 4        August 6, 2024.


 5   Q.   Please provide an overview of the Huntsbrook Project.

 6   A.   The Huntsbrook Project is a new 345 kV switching station that will enable the

 7        interconnection of up to 2,400 MW of new generation resources to the New England

 8        transmission system without necessitating significant other upgrades of the existing

 9        transmission system. The Huntsbrook Project is estimated to cost approximately $237

10        million. The Huntsbrook Project has a projected in-service date of December 2034.

11                The Huntsbrook Project is one component of a broader regional initiative known as

12        Power Up New England (“Power Up”), an integrated portfolio of projects developed

13        through a collaboration among project developers, including Eversource, ISO-NE, and the

14        six New England states to address the region’s evolving reliability and resource adequacy

15        needs. Power Up’s transmission investments include the Huntsbrook Project and the

16        Brayton Point Project in Massachusetts, which is being developed by National Grid. These

17        projects are designed to strategically prepare the transmission system for future generation

18        development by creating points of interconnection in advance of project-specific needs,

 2   Huntsbrook Project and the Brayton Point Project will ready the New England transmission

 4          Power Up also includes Form Energy’s Multi-Day Iron-Air Battery project, an 85

 5   MW/8,500 MWh advanced multi-day storage facility to be constructed in Maine. The

 6   facility will be capable of continuously dispatching electricity for 100 hours, providing up

 8   other system events. In addition to enhancing system reliability, the battery project will

 1   III.   DEVELOPMENT OF THE HUNTSBROOK PROJECT

 2   Q.     How does Eversource identify projects to meet New England’s future transmission

 3          needs?

 4   A.     Eversource engages in comprehensive long-term planning and analysis to help ensure that

 5          New England has a secure and reliable energy supply to meet increasing demand and a

 6          robust and modern transmission grid to integrate new generation resources and increase

 7          resilience to extreme weather.     Eversource’s planning seeks to reduce transmission

 8          congestion, support reliability and resource adequacy, contain transmission-related costs,

 9          and lower wholesale energy prices across New England.

10                   Through this proactive and integrated planning process, Eversource identifies,

11          among other things, locations on the transmission grid where new generation resources

12          could be interconnected at scale with relatively few upgrades and at low cost. These

13          locations are then analyzed by a cross-functional team of subject matter experts across the

14          Eversource transmission organization.       The team performs early-stage development

15          activities to understand, at a conceptual level, the required electrical elements, associated

16          physical space needs, wholesale market impacts, constructability considerations,

17          environmental licensing and permitting issues, siting and regulatory considerations, and

18          related regulatory and commercial impacts. In addition to power flow and economic

19          analyses, the cross-functional subject matter experts perform desktop analyses of the

20          identified locations to evaluate the practical and commercial feasibility of these emerging

21          transmission project concepts.

 1   Q.   How did Eversource identify the opportunity for a transmission project at the

 2        Huntsbrook Junction?

 3   A.   Through the process described above, Eversource’s team of cross-functional subject matter

 4        experts identified the Huntsbrook Junction location as an ideal transmission project concept

 5        to enable new generation interconnection. Further analysis confirmed the location to be

 6        strategically situated on the 345 kV transmission network with access to multiple

 7        transmission corridors. The combination of these factors made it an attractive point of

 8        interconnection for generation developers seeking to interconnect projects to the grid.

 9        Initial screening also confirmed that the specific location is beneficial because it is in a

10        wooded area, far from residential abutters, and on Eversource-owned property already used

11        to host transmission infrastructure. Finally, the Huntsbrook Junction concept performed

12        well in the team’s preliminary viability assessment.

               II. Methodology and Approach
This analysis uses power market and regional economic equilibrium modeling software and
assumptions to forecast wholesale electric energy market dynamics and impacts on the general
economy, respectively. The power market model forecasts power market dispatch, financial
outcomes, and transmission network usage for future years (i.e., 2033-2042) where the Project
would be placed into service. By comparing the results of representative futures with and without
the Project, the analysis provides insight into the potential impact that the Project would have
on power sector outcomes. The power market model is used to evaluate (i) congestion relief and
(ii) power market economic benefits afforded by the Project. The regional economic equilibrium
model is used to evaluate the broader regional economic impacts of the project, including the
impact of the hub construction spending and wholesale energy cost savings on employment,
gross domestic product, industry output, and personal income across the Eversource service
territory. The regional economic model translates the wholesale energy costs savings identified
by the PLEXOS model into their impact on business competitiveness, household purchasing
power, and economic activity across Connecticut, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire. The
assumptions included in the analysis are based on credible, third-party sources and are provided
for transparency.

             F. Regional Economic Equilibrium Assumptions
The REMI analysis is structured as two separate simulations, each representing a distinct
economic channel through which the project affects the regional economy. The first simulation
captures the one-time construction impact of the hub infrastructure. The second captures the
recurring energy-cost savings that each generation technology enables through lower regional
electricity prices. The two simulations were run independently to preserve the distinction
between short-term construction stimulus and long-term operational benefits, and to ensure
that the temporary nature of construction employment is clearly separated from the sustained
operational impact of the project on electricity cost.
    1. Construction Impact
The project’s hub construction budget was derived from the internal cost estimate prepared for
the DOE grant application. Approximately 13 percent of the total budget is allocated to
equipment purchases (high voltage transformers, switchgear, circuit breakers, etc.). Because this
equipment is manufactured by specialized firms outside the study region, the equipment line was
excluded from the REMI input to avoid overstating local supply-chain effects. The remaining
budget, representing contractor labor, supplies, professional services, and other direct and
indirect cost, was entered into REMI as exogenous production demand in the electric power
sector (NAICS 221100). Budget amounts were entered in nominal dollars. The REMI baseline
employment profile was applied, allowing the model to determine direct employment from the
spending level. The construction simulation is identical across all three technology scenarios.
    2. Operations and Cost Savings Impact
The wholesale energy cost-to-load savings produced by the PLEXOS analysis were aggregated by
state (CT, MA, NH) and allocated to three customer classes based on EIA electricity consumption
data. Each class was modeled through separate REMI policy variable reflecting the distinct
economic mechanisms through which businesses and households respond to electricity cost
changes.

The allocation reflects a fundamental difference in the way electricity price reductions affect the
regional economy. For commercial and industrial electricity users, a reduction in the wholesale
price of electricity lowers the cost of a key production input. This reduces the cost per unit of
output for businesses in the region, improving their competitive position relative to firms in other
states. As regional firms become more cost-competitive, they attract additional economic
activity, expand output, and support employment. The effect operates through the supply side
of the economy – lower input costs improve the region’s cost structure and competitive standing.
The commercial and industrial shares were modeled separately because these sectors face
different electricity intensities and different competitive dynamics. A hospital or office building
responds to lower energy costs differently than a manufacturing facility, and REMI’s internal
structure captures this differentiation when the inputs are separated.
For residential electricity users, a reduction in wholesale price lowers household electricity bills,
increasing disposable income. Households redirect this freed-up income toward other goods and
services, including food, housing, transportation, and retail. The impact operates through the
demand side of the economy – lower electricity expenditure supports consumer spending across
other sectors. These supply-side and demand-side channels operate independently within REMI’s
equation structure, and a dollar entering through one does not also enter through the other. The
three-way allocation therefore partitions the total cost savings without overlap.

                    c. Congestion Charges
The LMP has three components: energy, congestion, and losses. In PLEXOS, the congestion
charge is equal the congestion component of each LMP. When there is no congestion, the
congestion charge component of the LMP is equal to zero. In contrast, when congestion is
present, the congestion charge component of the LMP can either be a positive or negative
number, depending upon its location relative to the congestion. For example, the nodes within
an export- constrained location with surplus generation will likely have negative congestion
charges in the hours that congestion is present. Further, the nodes outside of an export-
constrained location with surplus generation will likely have positive congestion charges in hours
that congestion is present, reflecting an inability to access cheaper generation inside the export-
constrained location. To quantify the amount of congestion charges, it is necessary to consider
all nodes in all hours of the study horizon and to also consider how much load is at each of those
nodes. Accordingly, the analysis multiplies the load times the congestion charge at each node
over the study horizon to quantify the amount of both positive and negative congestion charges.

               2.      Operations and Cost Savings Impact
The operations phase measures the sustained economic value that each generation technology
delivers to the regional economy through lower wholesale electricity cost over the 2033 to 2042
study period. Unlike construction, where the economic mechanism is straightforward, the
operations phase impact works through price channels as new spending creates direct activity
that ripples through the supply chain. A reduction in wholesale electricity prices does not directly
hire workers or place orders with suppliers. It reduces the cost of doing business for commercial
and industrial firms and frees disposable income for households. These are second-order effects
that operate through regional competitiveness and consumer spending reallocation. As a result,
the employment effects from this channel are modest, and GDP and total output are the most
appropriate measures of economic benefit. The small employment numbers do not indicate that
the benefit is immaterial as they reflect the fact that the cost reduction is distributed across the

individual firm level. The operations-phase impact enters the economy through a reduction in
electricity costs, not through direct spending or hiring. When electricity prices fall, no employer

               VI. Conclusions and Findings
The Project is a new switching station at a new location capable of receiving an injection of power
from a range of representative resources of various resource types. The Project is designed to
enhance the capability and flexibility of the regional transmission system to accommodate a
range of future energy resources and evolving system needs. The New England states selected
the Project for inclusion in an application for federal funding that was submitted in April 2024.
The Project Reduces Consumer Costs and Relieves Congestion in Eastern Connecticut
The congestion-relief analysis evaluates the benefits of relocating a representative portfolio of
1,725 MW of generation and energy storage resources consisting of a 500 MW SMR, 525 MW
combined-cycle facility, and 700 MW BESS from Montville and Millstone to the proposed
Huntsbrook Junction switching station. Results indicate that relocating these resources improves
system efficiency, reduces transmission congestion, lowers wholesale electricity prices, and
provides meaningful customer savings across Connecticut and New England.
Key findings include:

       approximately 1,000 to 1,600 line-hours annually, improving overall system performance
       and operational flexibility.
   o Lower Wholesale Electricity Prices: The Project Case reduces average annual LMPs across
       all New England zones by approximately $1.5/MWh to $1.9/MWh, with Connecticut LMP
       reductions exceeding $2/MWh in later study years.
   o Lower Congestion Charges: The Project Case reduces total load-weighted congestion net
       charges (positive and negative) by approximately $10 million (nominal) or $7.8 million

   o Lower Production Costs: The Project Case reduces New England’s production cost by
       $48.5 million (nominal) or $37.9 million (2026 real dollars) on an average annual basis
       over the study horizon.
   o Customer Cost Savings: The Project Case reduces New England’s wholesale energy cost
       by $229.7 million (nominal) or $179.8 million (2026 real dollars) on an average annual
       basis. Over the 9-year horizon, this could result in cumulative reduction of $2.1 billion to
       consumers. Connecticut wholesale energy costs decline throughout the study horizon,
       generating approximately $16.8 million in average annual savings and $455 million in total
       nominal savings.
   o Regional Benefits: Customer savings are realized across all New England regions, ranging

  A new four-hour BESS enabled by the project provides operational flexibility by shifting energy

The Project Provides Economic Benefits to the Connecticut and New England Economy

The results demonstrate that the Huntsbrook Junction hub delivers measurable economic value
to the Eversource service territory under all three technology scenarios. The construction phase
alone generates 624 jobs and $222 million GDP, providing significant near-term economic
stimulus concentrated in Connecticut. The operations phase adds a layer of sustained, structural
economic benefit whose magnitude and reliability depend on the generation technology
connected to the hub. Dispatchable resources, whether gas-fired or nuclear, deliver consistent
and growing economic returns that improve the region's competitive position over the study
horizon. Battery storage delivers a positive but smaller and more variable return. At higher
capacity levels, the operations-phase contribution would represent a larger share of total project
value, further differentiating the technologies. The hub's flexibility to accommodate multiple
resource types positions it as enabling infrastructure that can deliver economic benefits to the
region regardless of how the generation portfolio evolves.
